title: India Ships the Harvest, Not the Meal: Value-Added Foods Still a Thin Slice of Food Exports
excerpt: Processed foods are only about a fifth of India's $50 billion-plus food exports, but Diwali demand and a ready-to-eat surge show where the value is moving.
body:
• Processed foods account for only about 20 percent of India's food exports of more than $50 billion, and value-added products make up less than 15 percent of the export basket, against 40-50 percent for peer exporters, according to the Deloitte-FICCI STEP UP report.
  • A Trade Promotion Council of India (TPCI) survey of overseas buyers found Diwali-season demand for Indian food up about 6 percent on average, and more than 15 percent in some markets, led by sweets, savories, rice, spices, pickles and ghee.
  • Ready-to-eat and ready-to-cook foods are the fastest-growing segment: India's exports of ready-to-eat and cooked products rose 16 percent to $2.4 billion in the financial year ended March 2026.
  • For diaspora shoppers, the shift means more shelf-stable Indian meals, festive mixes and branded packaged foods in mainstream US, Gulf and European supermarkets, not only in ethnic stores.

India is the world's largest producer of milk, spices and several other farm staples, and its food exports exceed $50 billion a year. Yet most of that trade still leaves the country close to its raw form. Processed foods contribute only about 20 percent of India's food exports, and value-added products account for less than 15 percent of the export basket, compared with 40-50 percent for peer exporting nations, according to the Deloitte India and FICCI "STEP UP" report launched at FICCI FoodWorld India 2026. The same raw material, the report notes, earns three to five times more when it is processed before export.

A processing sector that has grown, but not caught up

The base has expanded steadily. Government data cited by the Ministry of Food Processing Industries show the share of processed food in India's agri-food exports rose from 13.7 percent in 2014-15 to 20.4 percent in 2024-25, while gross value added in food processing climbed from Rs 1.34 lakh crore in 2014-15 to Rs 2.24 lakh crore in 2023-24, per India Seatrade News. The sector drew $7.33 billion in foreign direct investment between April 2014 and March 2025 and accounts for 12.83 percent of employment in registered manufacturing. Deloitte and FICCI estimate the domestic processed-food opportunity at nearly $600 billion by 2030. The export mix, however, still tilts toward commodities such as rice and raw spices rather than branded, packaged products.

Diwali demand shows where the growth is

The clearest current demand signal comes from the festive season. A survey of international buyers by the Trade Promotion Council of India found average demand growth of about 6 percent ahead of Diwali, with some markets recording increases above 15 percent, South Asian Herald reported. Traditional products led procurement: sweets, savories, rice, spices, pickles and ghee, including kaju katli, laddoo, halwa, bhujia, mixture and murukku. Gulf markets drove much of the seasonal buying, with Kuwait sourcing sweets, ghee, paneer, beverages, condiments and dry fruits, Oman buying rice, spices, masalas and pulses, and Bahrain ordering festive foods and savories. India's food and beverage exports to the United Arab Emirates rose from $2.3 billion in 2021 to $3.6 billion in 2025, a compound annual growth rate of 11.3 percent, according to TPCI.

Convenience foods are breaking out of the diaspora aisle

The faster growth sits in convenience formats. A German importer reported roughly 25 percent year-on-year growth in ready-to-eat imports and a Kuwaiti buyer reported 28 percent, TPCI said. India's exports of ready-to-eat and cooked food products rose 16 percent to $2.4 billion in the financial year ended March 2026, from $2.1 billion a year earlier. Processed food exports overall grew about 10 percent year on year, with processed fruits and vegetables, cereal preparations and dairy and poultry products among the stronger categories, the Deloitte-FICCI report found. European buyers are sourcing Indian ready-to-eat, frozen, organic and vegan lines for mainstream retail and foodservice, a shift TPCI says is moving Indian packaged food beyond diaspora-led demand. "With global consumers actively seeking authentic ethnic flavors, healthier options, and convenience, India is uniquely positioned to become a reliable hub for value-added food products," TPCI Chairman Mohit Singla said.

Freight, compliance and shelf life remain the brakes

Exporters and buyers surveyed by TPCI cited high freight and container costs, customs inspection delays, food-safety and import-compliance requirements, limited shelf life and geopolitical instability as their main concerns. Disruption on West Asian shipping routes poses a specific risk for Gulf-bound festive and perishable shipments. Meeting European food-safety, labelling and certification standards requires investment in packaging, shelf-life technology, cold chains and testing that many small processors have yet to make. Until that investment lands at scale, India's food export story remains one of volume first and value second: the harvest ships out, and much of the margin is earned elsewhere.
